items.streamTitle: Communication changed the pattern of crowd decisions without shortening the time to reach them
items.streamSummary: An experiment with 444 people in small and larger anonymous crowds tested movement decisions under uncertainty, with or without verbal communication. Communication did not significantly shorten the time to reach a final arrangement. It could be associated with either strong agreement or polarization, while fully uniform outcomes were uncommon without speech. The intended shared-identity manipulation did not work, and there were too few group runs to support strong conclusions about all decision distributions. The study is useful because it challenges the idea that communication simply accelerates crowd consensus.

items.streamTitle: Tesla's European FSD safety evidence did not support its strongest life-saving claims, outside researchers told Reuters
items.streamSummary: A Reuters investigation reviewed Tesla's European FSD safety studies, regulatory correspondence, and assessments from seven traffic-safety researchers. Because the company had too few European FSD miles for a meaningful crash-rate comparison, it relied on surrogate behaviors such as hard braking, horn use, turn signals, acceleration, and cornering. Researchers said several proxies were weak and the evidence did not show that FSD prevents fatal crashes; Tesla's own study cautioned that the comparisons were not causal estimates. Reuters also documented pressure on Dutch regulators, who said their review remained independent. The case highlights the difference between measured proxies and validated safety outcomes.

items.streamTitle: U.S. voters showed broad concern about AI jobs, regulation, data centers, and military targeting
items.streamSummary: A nationwide Reuters/Ipsos survey of 4,506 adults found broad concern about AI across party lines. Among registered voters, 57% said the administration was not taking AI risks seriously enough, 84% saw AI as a threat to American workers, and majorities of Democrats and Republicans supported stricter regulation. Fifty-six percent backed limits on data-center construction, while 57% opposed using AI to determine military-strike targets, up from 49% in an August 2025 poll. The survey captures current attitudes, not how voters would respond to detailed policy tradeoffs or how concerns translate into behavior.

items.streamTitle: Satiety did not reliably silence attention to high-calorie foods, and BMI changed the pattern
items.streamSummary: Two attentional-blink experiments tested whether hunger, satiety, BMI, and recent food consumption change automatic capture by high-calorie food cues. Food distractors reliably disrupted target detection. After satiation, attention to novel foods declined in normal-weight participants but remained robust among participants with overweight or obesity; cues for foods that had just been eaten continued to capture attention in both groups. The findings do not show that attention causes overeating, but they demonstrate that satiety alone is not a simple off-switch for food-cue salience and that context changes the observed bias.
items.attribution: Ballestero-Arnau, Rodríguez-Herreros & Cunillera — International Journal of Obesity

items.streamTitle: NATO is using STEADFAST DUEL 2026 to test Article 5 command structures, cognitive warfare, and AI-enabled training
items.streamSummary: STEADFAST DUEL 2026 brings about 8,000 personnel and all 32 NATO Allies into the Alliance's largest annual computer-assisted command-post exercise. The Article 5 scenario tests multi-domain command and control across land, air, maritime, space, cyber, electronic warfare, logistics, CBRN defense, and civil-military coordination. NATO is also using the event to experiment with cognitive warfare, escalation dynamics, and its Maven Smart System. The exercise demonstrates an integrated testing environment, not yet improved readiness: public results on decision quality, interoperability, or operational effect have not been reported.

items.streamTitle: Personalized influenza-risk messages raised actual vaccination in three field trials
items.streamSummary: Three randomized US field trials involving over 90,000 patients found modest increases in recorded influenza vaccination after personalized risk messages. Explaining or disclosing the algorithm added no clear benefit.
items.attribution: Rosenbaum et al. — Nature Human Behaviour (randomized field trials)

items.streamTitle: Hospital contract rules redirected incentives toward more public patients, with a possible quality tradeoff
items.streamSummary: Using 2.3 million Irish inpatient records, researchers examined a 2014 reform that let public hospitals place private patients in public wards while consultant contracts required three or four additional public patients for each private patient. The private-patient share did not increase. Instead, consultants treated more public patients and shortened stays for both groups. The authors interpret the contract ratio as an important constraint on behavior, while warning that faster throughput may have reduced care quality for public patients. The study shows why incentive evaluation must track adaptation across several outcomes, not just the behavior directly regulated.
items.attribution: Guo et al. — Nature Human Behaviour

items.streamTitle: Arm-structured policies improved dual-arm robot generalization, while absolute success remained limited
items.streamSummary: ACG-Bench tests whether dual-arm robots can recombine familiar per-arm skills in unseen orders and timing relationships. An architecture combining skill-specific adapters and arm-wise attention reached 21.53% success on unseen simulated compositions versus 5.53% for the strongest baseline, and 39% on five physical-robot conditions versus 10% for the strongest baseline. The relative improvement is substantial, but most unseen physical trials still failed. The study therefore supports arm-aware architectural structure as a promising generalization strategy without implying that dual-arm compositional autonomy is solved.

items.streamTitle: Pre-action boundary auditing blocked substantially more staged prompt injections in long-horizon agents
items.streamSummary: Researchers generated staged prompt-injection attacks that propagate through multi-step Claude Code and Codex workflows and only become harmful at a later consequential action. They then audited the pending message or tool call immediately before execution. On a 479-pair benchmark, Path-Aligned Attribution reached 86% block recall at a 6–8% false-block rate, compared with 44–47% recall and 16–33% false-block rates for ARGUS under the same backend. The work is preprint-stage, but it supports a clear security pattern: trace where action parameters came from and gate external effects at the execution boundary.

items.streamTitle: ForkPilot learned when agents should backtrack and cut token use by as much as 59%
items.streamSummary: ForkPilot treats retrospective search in long-horizon agents as a changing cost–benefit decision rather than a fixed behavior. It learns from completed trajectories which earlier branches were worth revisiting, then updates that policy as new executions accumulate. Across six benchmarks, seven model families, and nine baselines, the authors report state-of-the-art-comparable performance with token reductions of up to 59.2%. The work is preprint-stage and benchmark-dependent, but it highlights a practical agent-design principle: recovery, re-search, and self-correction should be allocated selectively rather than invoked uniformly.

items.streamTitle: Behavioral history beat demographics and personality for predicting individual synthetic-persona choices
items.streamSummary: A two-wave study of 845 U.S. adults tested what information helps LLM synthetic personas reproduce a particular person's later decisions across 14 behavioral biases. Demographics, personality, and cognitive descriptions produced population averages that looked human-like but captured only 7–12% of human test–retest informedness at the individual level. Supplying earlier behavioral choices raised that figure to as much as 28% and restored between-person variance much more effectively. The result supports behavioral history as a stronger persona scaffold, while also showing that even richer synthetic personas remain weak substitutes for specific individuals.

items.streamTitle: South Korea said AI appeared to have been used in bank hacks, while specifics remained under investigation
items.streamSummary: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said artificial intelligence appeared to have been used in recent cyberattacks on commercial banks and ordered a rapid investigation. At that stage, the specific AI tools, attacker identity, and extent of compromise were not publicly established. The item is evidence of an official assessment and active investigation, not yet a completed forensic attribution.

items.streamTitle: Drone attacks on merchant ships in Bulgaria's EEZ were confirmed while attribution remained uncertain
items.streamSummary: Reuters reported two merchant vessels struck by drones in Bulgaria's Black Sea exclusive economic zone, including one that sank. The incidents were confirmed, but responsibility was not independently established at the time; Ukrainian officials blamed Russia while Moscow had not commented. The case illustrates the need to preserve attribution uncertainty even when physical effects are clear.

items.streamTitle: Cognitive offloading made remembered information less neurally decodable
items.streamSummary: An fMRI study found that information participants expected to recover from an external reminder became less decodable in brain activity, resembling deliberate-forgetting conditions in some analyses. The result supports cognitive offloading as a change in how information is maintained, not proof that memory is simply deleted. External support can alter internal representation even when task performance remains adequate.

items.streamTitle: MLB umpire count bias fit a Bayesian uncertainty model
items.streamSummary: A large analysis of MLB pitch calls found that count-dependent differences were consistent with Bayesian prior expectations, especially among umpires with greater perceptual uncertainty. The result does not make every biased call optimal, but it shows that systematic judgment shifts can arise from uncertainty-sensitive inference rather than one simple heuristic. Intervention design should target the process actually producing the bias.

items.streamTitle: A security paper was retracted after its code lacked claimed core components
items.streamSummary: A Scientific Reports retraction found that the available code did not contain key components described in the paper, including claimed security mechanisms. The case shows that 'code available' is not equivalent to reproducibility. Technical claims need traceable implementation, executable tests, and evidence that the published artifact actually corresponds to the described method.

items.streamTitle: Six minutes of HIIT improved selected executive-function measures, not inhibitory control
items.streamSummary: A randomized study found that a six-minute high-intensity exercise bout improved working-memory response speed and supported one cognitive-flexibility outcome, while inhibitory control did not significantly improve. The mixed result is more informative than a broad 'exercise boosts cognition' claim. Immediate task effects also do not establish lasting academic or behavioral benefit.

items.streamTitle: An LLM reporting checker reached useful accuracy, with evidence retrieval still a bottleneck
items.streamSummary: A npj Digital Medicine study developed an automated system for checking clinical-trial reports against SPIRIT and CONSORT elements. It achieved F1 around 0.822 in the reported evaluation. The work shows promise for scalable reporting review, but errors in retrieving the relevant passage can propagate into the final judgment. Human review and traceable evidence remain important.
items.attribution: Jiang et al. — npj Digital Medicine

items.streamTitle: Combining temporal dependence and higher-order statistics improved linear causal discovery in simulations
items.streamSummary: A causal-discovery preprint combined temporal dependence with higher-order statistics and reported improved graph recovery in simulations plus more stable directional results in an fMRI application. The method is promising when its assumptions are plausible, but it does not provide assumption-free causal identification. Linear structure, acyclicity, and measurement quality remain central.

items.streamTitle: A hybrid ML-and-physics pipeline found trace-gas plumes missed by human review
items.streamSummary: Researchers combined machine-learning plume detection with physics-based spectroscopic fitting on EMIT imagery. The system identified large emissions with few false positives and suggested that at least a quarter of large plumes in the evaluated data had been missed by earlier human review. The result is a strong example of using AI for candidate detection while preserving an independent physical verification step.

items.streamTitle: EvoRiskBench found agent security varied sharply by the model–harness combination
items.streamSummary: EvoRiskBench evaluated 450 adversarial tasks across nine model and agent-harness configurations. Attack success differed substantially by the combination, reaching 68.44% for the most vulnerable tested setup. The benchmark does not estimate real-world incident frequency, but it demonstrates that security depends on tool execution, permissions, and orchestration as well as the underlying model.

items.streamTitle: Germany's BND warned that Russia's 'shadow war' raises the risk of violent conflict
items.streamSummary: Germany's foreign-intelligence chief warned that Russian hybrid activity had created a more dangerous confrontation and a real risk of violent conflict. He cited cyber and drone activity while stopping short of predicting an imminent large-scale attack on NATO. The statement is a strategic intelligence assessment, not a measured probability or proof of Moscow's intent.

items.streamTitle: The Army tested counter-drone systems at the southern border amid hundreds of reported incursions
items.streamSummary: Reuters reported U.S. Army counter-UAS testing in Arizona as cartel drone activity increased. Officials cited 378 incursions in the prior month and 11 drones downed by laser systems since August. The exercise tested a range of detection and defeat technologies, but public reporting did not establish comparative effectiveness across vendors or conditions. Field testing is an activity milestone, not a complete effectiveness assessment.

items.streamTitle: Truncating chatbot responses changed measured crisis-guidance performance
items.streamSummary: A Scientific Reports audit of mental-health chatbots found that response truncation could substantially change whether crisis guidance was detected, and that cultural keywords were not sufficient evidence of culturally adequate support. The study shows that evaluation design—including how much of an answer is retained—can materially alter safety conclusions.
